DocumentInfo.Title: Stage 1 - Revenue and Sales Strategy Analysis
DocumentInfo.Subtitle: Direct Sales Revenue Concentration and Programmatic Performance Review

ExecutiveSummary.Headline: We earned $10.3M in 18 months. But $3.5M of that came from advertisers who have not come back. We are replacing churn at only 18 cents on the dollar. That is a revenue crisis hiding behind a decent topline number.

Item.label: Revenue from Churned Advertisers (spent 2025, not back in 2026)

Section1_RevenueOverview.Title: OVERALL REVENUE PERFORMANCE
Section1_RevenueOverview.Narrative: The business generated $10.3M across direct, programmatic, and house channels over six quarters. Direct sales is the engine. Programmatic is underperforming relative to the impressions it serves. House ads represent wasted inventory that earns nearly nothing.
Section1_RevenueOverview.Insight: Direct earns $19.73 per thousand impressions. Programmatic earns $1.99. That is a 10x gap. Every impression that goes to programmatic instead of a direct deal costs us roughly $17.74 per thousand in lost revenue. This is the single biggest yield lever available.

Q4 2025 was the best quarter at $3.2M total. It also had the fewest total impressions (209M). Why? Direct campaigns consumed the inventory at premium rates. When direct is full, everything works. When it is not, programmatic fills at pennies.
House ads served 160 million impressions over this period. At even $2 eCPM, that is $320,000 in lost revenue. At $5 eCPM, it is $800,000. House ads should never exceed 5% of total impressions.

Section2_DirectSales_AdvertiserSegmentat.Title: DIRECT SALES - ADVERTISER SEGMENTATION
Section2_DirectSales_AdvertiserSegmentat.Narrative: We classified every direct advertiser into five categories based on their spending behavior across Q1 2025 through Q2 2026. This tells us who is reliable, who left, who is new, and who came once and vanished. The picture is not comforting.

Category1_AlwaysOn.Label: ALWAYS-ON: Active in both 2025 AND 2026 across multiple quarters
Category1_AlwaysOn.Description: These are the backbone. They keep spending. They trust us. Protect them at all costs.

Category2_Churned.Label: CHURNED: Spent in 2025, zero activity in 2026
Category2_Churned.Description: This is the alarm bell. These advertisers gave us money last year and have not returned. Every single one is a sales call waiting to happen. The longer we wait, the harder the reactivation.
Category2_Churned.ShareOfTotal: 40.4% of all direct revenue came from advertisers who are now gone

Section3_NewAdvertisers2026.Title: NEW IN 2026: First-time spenders not seen in 2025
Section3_NewAdvertisers2026.Description: These are the net new logos sales brought in. Good sign that the pipeline is alive. Bad sign that the total volume does not come close to replacing what we lost.
Section3_NewAdvertisers2026.ReplacementRatio: For every $1 we lost to churn, we replaced only $0.18 with new business

Section4_OneTimeSpenders.Title: ONE-TIME SPENDERS: Appeared in only one quarter ever
Section4_OneTimeSpenders.Description: These advertisers came in, spent, and vanished. Either the campaign did not perform, the relationship was transactional, or nobody followed up. Each one is a conversation that did not happen.
Section4_OneTimeSpenders.Insight: Finance and Pharma dominate the one-time list. These are verticals with budget. They tested us and did not come back. That is either a performance issue, a relationship issue, or a follow-up issue. We need to know which.

Section5_RepeatedButLapsed.Title: REPEATED BUT LAPSED: Spent 2 to 3 quarters, then stopped
Section5_RepeatedButLapsed.Description: These had momentum. They came back at least once. Something broke the pattern. These are the warmest reactivation leads because they already proved willingness to repeat.

Section6_RevenueConcentration.Title: REVENUE CONCENTRATION - TOP 10 ANALYSIS
Section6_RevenueConcentration.Description: How dependent are we on a handful of advertisers? If any of the top 10 walks away tomorrow, what happens to the business?

ConcentrationMetrics.Metric: 4 of 10 (American Family, Celebrity Cruises, Ally, LinkedIn)

Section6_RevenueConcentration.Insight: Half our revenue sits with 10 advertisers. Four of those 10 are already gone. That means 15.7% of our historical direct revenue no longer has a source. This is not a future risk. This is a current reality.

Section7_ProgrammaticAnalysis.Title: PROGRAMMATIC REVENUE - PARTNER PERFORMANCE
Section7_ProgrammaticAnalysis.Narrative: Programmatic contributes 15.5% of revenue but consumes 57% of impressions. The yield is terrible relative to direct. Media Mint manages this channel. We need answers.

ProgrammaticConcentration.Assessment: Extremely concentrated. One partner policy change away from losing 38% of programmatic revenue.

Q4_2025_Crash.Title: THE Q4 2025 PROGRAMMATIC COLLAPSE
Q4_2025_Crash.LikelyExplanation: Q4 2025 had the highest direct revenue ever ($3.1M). Direct campaigns consumed available inventory, leaving minimal remnant for programmatic. This is not necessarily bad if direct is paying 10x the CPM. But we need to confirm this with Media Mint.
Q4_2025_Crash.QuestionForMediaMint: Was the Q4 drop purely an inventory availability issue, or were there also demand-side problems, floor price changes, or partner technical issues?

AdExchangeAdvertiserDetail.Title: Who is buying through Ad Exchange (Programmatic Demand)
AdExchangeAdvertiserDetail.Description: These are advertisers spending programmatically. Some of them could potentially be converted to direct deals at higher CPMs.
AdExchangeAdvertiserDetail.Insight: AT and T, Kering, Comcast, Goldman Sachs, and GM Group are all spending programmatically at $2 CPM when they could be approached for direct deals at $15-25 CPM. That is a direct-to-programmatic conversion opportunity.

Section8_YieldAnalysis.Title: YIELD AND EFFICIENCY METRICS

Metric.label: Direct takes 31% of impressions but earns 84% of revenue
Programmatic takes 57% of impressions but earns 15.5% of revenue
House takes 11.5% of impressions and earns 0.5% of revenue

Section8_YieldAnalysis.Insight: Q4 2025 proves the model. Fewer impressions, higher eCPM, more revenue. The goal is not to serve more impressions. The goal is to sell more inventory at direct rates. Every 10 million impressions shifted from programmatic to direct is worth an additional $177,400 in revenue.

Action.What: Reactivate the 4 churned top-10 advertisers: American Family Insurance, Celebrity Cruises, Ally Financial, LinkedIn Marketing Solutions
Action.Why: These 4 alone represent 15.7% of all historical direct revenue. Even converting 2 of them back at 50% of prior spend recovers $340K
Action.Who: Sales team with AdOps support on inventory proposals

Action.What: Run a reactivation campaign targeting all 34 churned advertisers with custom inventory packages
Action.Why: $3.5M in revenue vanished. Even a 15-20% reactivation rate brings back $500K-700K
Action.Who: Sales team with specific proposals based on their original placements

Action.What: Convert new 2026 big spenders (TIAA, JPMorgan, Reliance, Target) to multi-quarter commitments NOW before they become one-timers
Action.Why: The pattern is clear - advertisers come once and leave. We must lock them in while they are warm
Action.Who: Account management with long-term deal structures

Action.What: Approach programmatic advertisers (AT and T, Kering, Goldman Sachs, Comcast, GM Group) for direct deals
Action.Why: They are already on our site at $2 CPM. Offer them premium placements at $15-20 CPM with guaranteed viewability and placement
Action.Who: Sales with programmatic buyer contact info from Media Mint

Action.What: Create a loyalty framework for Always-On advertisers (Rolex, Toyota, HP, Novartis, P and G) with annual deal incentives
Action.Why: Losing even one of these is catastrophic. Rolex alone is 10% of direct revenue

Action.What: Demand a full audit from Media Mint on the Q4 2025 collapse and current recovery plan
Action.Why: We lost $257K in one quarter. Even accounting for direct inventory consumption, the drop is disproportionate

Action.What: Diversify away from Media.net dependency - add 2 to 3 new header bidding partners
Action.Why: 38.5% of programmatic revenue in one partner is dangerous. Media.net already dropped 47% YoY

Action.What: Kill Magnite and SimpleFeed from the programmatic stack
Action.Why: Combined $0 in recent quarters. They add latency and complexity for zero return

Action.What: Investigate and activate Preferred Deals properly
Action.Why: Only $146 total in Preferred Deals over 18 months. This channel is essentially unused but can yield $5+ eCPM

Action.What: Reduce house ad impressions from 12% average to under 5%
Action.Why: 160 million house impressions over 18 months. At even $2 eCPM that is $320K left on the table

Action.What: Map available inventory from churned advertisers and create sales packages
Action.Why: When Celebrity Cruises, Ally, LinkedIn left, their placements went to remnant. Package and re-sell them

Action.What: Push more inventory into Sponsorship format versus Standard
Action.Why: Sponsorship eCPM is $27.56 versus Standard at $17.73. A 10% shift to Sponsorship adds $1M+ annually at current volumes

Section10_QuestionsForBoss.Title: QUESTIONS THAT NEED ANSWERS BEFORE STAGE 2
Section10_QuestionsForBoss.Question: Do we have advertiser vertical or industry tags in GAM? I need to do a vertical concentration analysis to identify which industries are underrepresented and where sales should focus prospecting.
Can we get the contract end dates and IO terms for the top 20 active advertisers? I need to know which renewals are coming up in the next 90 days so we can flag them as retention priorities.
Does Media Mint have a formal explanation for the Q4 2025 programmatic collapse? Was it purely inventory availability, or were there demand-side, floor price, or technical issues?
What is our fill rate by ad unit right now? I need to identify which specific placements have unsold inventory so we can package them for new advertiser pitches.
Do we have audience segment data connected? If we can show advertisers our audience composition, it strengthens the pitch for higher CPMs and new verticals.
For the churned advertisers, does the sales team know WHY they left? Was it performance, budget cuts, agency change, or simply no follow-up? The answer changes the reactivation strategy completely.
What is the sales team target for new logos in 2026? We brought in $647K from new advertisers but lost $3.5M from churn. Is there a pipeline number we should be benchmarking against?

Are there programmatic advertiser contacts available through Media Mint? Specifically for AT and T, Kering, Goldman Sachs, and Comcast who are spending programmatically and could be approached for direct deals.
Should we be looking at device-level or geo-level breakdowns? Different devices and geographies have different yield profiles, and it may reveal where we are leaving money on the table.
What is the total available inventory forecast for Q3 and Q4 2026? I need to quantify exactly how much room we have to accommodate new advertisers without displacing existing ones.

Section11_WhatComesNext.Title: STAGE 2 PLAN - WHAT WE BUILD NEXT
Section11_WhatComesNext.NextStep: Vertical analysis - Once we tag advertisers by industry, we identify gap verticals to target
Inventory availability map - Which ad units have capacity for new campaigns
Pricing strategy - Are we underpricing? Competitive CPM benchmarking
90-day reactivation plan - Specific outreach plan per churned advertiser with custom proposals
Media Mint accountability framework - KPIs and targets for programmatic optimization
Client-facing dashboard brief - Handoff to data team for visualization build
